5340:
When you entangle something, you cause it to get caught up, twisted, or trapped in something else — in a way that makes it very hard to break free. The key idea is not just being "stuck," but being stuck in a complicated, messy, intertwined way.

Think of a fish caught in a net. The more it struggles, the more the net wraps around it. That's the essence of entangle — something gets drawn into a situation where escape is difficult.

1. The Literal (Physical) Meaning

In its most direct sense, to entangle means to physically catch or twist something in another thing.

  • A bird gets entangled in a wire fence, its wings caught between the wires.
  • Seaweed entangles a swimmer's legs in the ocean.
  • Your headphone cord entangles itself around the leg of a chair.

The object is physically wrapped up, caught, or intertwined with something, and cannot easily pull away.

2. The Figurative (Abstract) Meaning

This is where the word truly lives and breathes in everyday language. To entangle someone (or yourself) figuratively means to draw them into a complicated, difficult, or troublesome situation — often one that is hard to get out of.

  • She became entangled in a legal dispute that lasted for years.
  • He slowly entangled himself in a web of lies that became impossible to maintain.
  • The company got entangled in a corruption scandal.
  • Their brief friendship entangled them in each other's problems.

Notice: in every case, there is a sense of being pulled in, of things becoming complicated and hard to undo, and of difficulty in getting free.

This is important. "Entangle" is not a neutral word. It carries a quiet sense of trouble, complication, and constraint. You don't hear someone say "I got entangled in a wonderful adventure." The word tends to appear when a situation is:

  • Unwanted — the person often didn't choose to be in it, or didn't realize it would become so difficult.
  • Complex — not just a simple problem, but one with many threads pulling in different directions.
  • Difficult to escape — like threads wrapped multiple times, you can't just step out easily.

So when you choose the word "entangle," you are also signaling that something went wrong, or that a situation became messy and binding.

a) To entangle something/someone in something:

The storm entangled the boat's anchor in the coral reef.
His ambition entangled him in relationships he couldn't manage.

b) To become entangled in something (passive/reflexive):

She became entangled in a bureaucratic nightmare.
The rope had become entangled around the propeller.

c) To entangle two things together:

The threads were so entangled together that separating them took hours.
Their lives were now deeply entangled with each other.

You will see entangled (adjective) very often, describing the state of being caught:

  • "The kite was entangled in the tree."
  • "He felt completely entangled in her problems."
  • "Their finances were deeply entangled."

The adjective "entangled" describes the result — the state of being caught up in something complex.

The noun entanglement means the situation or condition of being entangled:

  • "The country sought to avoid any foreign entanglement." (A classic use — meaning getting pulled into another country's conflicts.)
  • "Their romantic entanglement ended badly."
  • "The entanglement of wires under the desk was impossible to sort out."
Words Close in Meaning — and How They Differ

WordHow it's similarHow it's different
TrapGetting caught in somethingImplies a deliberate setup by someone; more about being caught than being twisted/complex
SnareBeing caughtOften implies someone set a trap intentionally; less about complexity
EnmeshVery close in meaningFocuses on being caught like in a mesh or net; slightly more formal
EmbroilGetting drawn into a conflict/messSpecifically about quarrels, controversies, or conflicts; more intense and combative than entangle
InvolveBeing connected to somethingMuch weaker; "involve" doesn't carry the sense of being trapped or unable to leave

So entangle sits at the intersection of complexity, being trapped, and difficulty escaping — it's more specific than "involve," more about intertwining than "trap," and broader than "embroil."

The direct opposite of entangle is disentangle — to carefully separate or free something from what it was caught in.

  • "She patiently disentangled the necklace chains."
  • "It took years to disentangle himself from that company's debts."
  • "The investigator worked to disentangle fact from fiction."

Disentangle implies careful, deliberate effort to undo the mess — reinforcing the idea that entanglements are not easy to reverse.

To entangle is to pull something into a complicated, twisted, trapped situation — physically or figuratively — from which getting free is difficult. The word always carries a tone of complication and constraint. The more entangled something is, the harder it is to separate or escape. Its closest companion words are entangled (the trapped state), entanglement (the situation itself), and disentangle (to work free of it).

When you see or use this word, think of threads wrapping around each other — messy, intertwined, and stubborn.
5341:
"Enter into" means to begin something in a serious, committed, or deeply involved way — not just to start it lightly, but to truly step inside it and become part of it.

Think of the two words separately for a moment. "Enter" means to go in or begin something. "Into" adds the sense of depth and direction — it suggests movement toward the inside of something, not just touching the surface. When you put them together, "enter into" captures the idea of going past the beginning point and becoming genuinely engaged, involved, or committed to something.

This is why "enter into" almost never describes physical movement into a room or building. It describes something more abstract — agreements, discussions, relationships, feelings, and situations that you become a real part of.
Meaning 1: To Formally Begin Something (The Most Common Use)

The most frequent and important meaning of "enter into" is to formally start or begin something together, usually between two or more parties. This something is typically an agreement, a contract, a negotiation, a relationship, or a partnership.

For example: "The two companies entered into a contract." This means the two companies formally began a contract together — they committed to it, and now they are bound by it. Similarly, "The countries entered into peace negotiations" means the countries formally started the process of negotiating peace. Other natural examples: "They entered into a business partnership," "She entered into a marriage," and "The government entered into a trade deal with its neighbor."

Notice that this meaning almost always involves more than one person or party, because you cannot enter into an agreement alone. It also carries a sense of seriousness and formality — you wouldn't use "entered into" for something trivial. It implies a commitment has been made and something significant has begun.
Meaning 2: To Begin Discussing or Examining Something

"Enter into" can also mean to start talking about, debating, or exploring a particular topic or subject. Here, you are not entering a physical space — you are entering a conversation, an argument, or a line of thought.

For example: "Let's not enter into the details right now" means "let's not start going through all the specifics at this moment." Similarly, "She refused to enter into a discussion about money" means she refused to start or get involved in that conversation.

This use appears very commonly in the negative form — meaning people use it to say they don't want to discuss something. When someone says "I'd rather not enter into that," they mean "I'd prefer not to get into that topic." Other examples: "I don't want to enter into this argument with you," and "He was not willing to enter into a debate on the matter."

You could replace "enter into" in these sentences with "get into" in informal speech, and the meaning would be the same. But "enter into" sounds more formal and deliberate.
Meaning 3: To Be a Factor In or Play a Role In Something

This is a subtler but elegant meaning. Here, a thing or idea (not a person) "enters into" a situation, meaning it plays a role, acts as an influence, or becomes a relevant factor.

For example: "Luck enters into every competition" means luck plays a role in every competition — it is a factor you cannot ignore. "Personal feelings should not enter into a professional decision" means personal feelings should not influence or play a part in a business decision. Other examples: "Many variables enter into the final calculation," and "Money always enters into these decisions."

This use is very elegant because instead of saying "Money is a factor in these decisions" or "Money plays a role," you can simply say "Money enters into these decisions." The phrase implies that the thing quietly but genuinely comes into the picture and affects the outcome.
Meaning 4: To Deeply Understand or Share In Someone's Feelings (Literary Use)

This is a more old-fashioned or literary meaning, but one you will encounter in books, formal writing, and classic texts. Here, "enter into" means to truly understand, feel, or share in someone else's emotions, spirit, or perspective — to go inside their experience and connect with it genuinely.

For example: "A great actor must enter into the feelings of the character" means the actor must truly feel and experience what the character feels — not just pretend from the outside, but genuinely connect with it from within. Similarly, "He found it difficult to enter into her grief" means he found it hard to truly understand and share in what she was feeling. Other examples: "She tried to enter into the festive spirit," and "He couldn't enter into the enthusiasm of his colleagues."

You can think of this use as meaning "to step inside someone's world and experience it as they do." It is a beautiful and precise phrase for something that is otherwise hard to describe concisely.

This is a point many learners get confused about, so it deserves careful attention.

For physical places, we use "enter" alone, not "enter into." You say "She entered the room" — not "She entered into the room." Saying "entered into the room" sounds old-fashioned, incorrect, or at least very unusual in modern English. "Enter" by itself is enough for physical movement.

For formal agreements and commitments, both "enter" and "enter into" are grammatically correct, but they carry a slight difference in feel. "They entered a contract" is acceptable, but "They entered into a contract" sounds more formal, more deliberate, and more emphatic about the fact that a real commitment is now underway.

For discussions and topics (Meaning 2), "enter into" is the standard phrase. "Let's not enter into this" is the natural expression. Saying "let's not enter this" in the same context would sound incomplete or odd.

For factors and influences (Meaning 3), only "enter into" works. You say "Luck enters into every game." You cannot say "Luck enters every game" and convey the same idea.

The essential difference is this: "enter" is about going in; "enter into" is about becoming truly involved, engaged, or committed. "Enter into" always has that extra layer of depth.
Common Words That Naturally Go With "Enter Into"

Certain nouns pair with "enter into" so naturally and frequently that they almost feel like set expressions. Knowing these combinations will help you recognize and use the phrase confidently.

In the context of formal agreements: enter into an agreement, enter into a contract, enter into a deal, enter into a partnership, enter into a treaty, enter into a marriage. In the context of conversation and debate: enter into a discussion, enter into a debate, enter into an argument, enter into negotiations, enter into a conversation, enter into details. In the context of feelings and atmosphere: enter into the spirit of something, enter into the feelings of someone.

All of these are used without "the" or "a" in some contexts and with them in others, depending on whether you are speaking generally or specifically — for example, both "enter into negotiations" (general) and "enter into the negotiations" (referring to specific, already-known negotiations) are perfectly correct.

"Enter into" leans decidedly formal. You will encounter it most in legal documents, business communication, news reporting, diplomatic language, and academic or literary writing. It is the language of contracts, diplomacy, and serious commitment.

In everyday casual speech, people tend to reach for simpler alternatives. Instead of "enter into a discussion," someone might say "get into a discussion." Instead of "enter into an agreement," they might say "make a deal." Instead of "enter into the spirit," they might say "get into the spirit."

This means that while "enter into" might not be a phrase you hear constantly in casual conversation, you will absolutely encounter it in formal reading and writing. And using it correctly in your own formal writing will make your English sound polished, precise, and sophisticated.

"Enter into" has four distinct meanings, but they all revolve around the same central idea: going past the surface and becoming truly involved, committed, or engaged with something.

The first and most common meaning is to formally begin something together, such as a contract, an agreement, a negotiation, or a relationship. The second meaning is to start discussing or examining a topic, and this is especially common in the negative — "I don't want to enter into that." The third meaning is for a thing or factor to play a role in a situation — "luck enters into every game." The fourth meaning, which is literary, is to genuinely understand or share in someone's feelings or the spirit of something.

The phrase almost never describes physical movement into a place — that is the job of "enter" alone. "Enter into" always carries that extra sense of depth, formality, and genuine involvement. It is precise, elegant, and once you understand it fully, you will begin to notice it everywhere in formal English.
5342: To enter the fray means to join a fight, argument, competition, or any intense struggle that is already going on.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Before you understand the idiom as a whole, it helps to understand its two parts:

"Fray" is the key word here. It comes from an old English/French word meaning a noisy, chaotic fight or battle. Think of soldiers clashing on a battlefield — shouting, weapons clashing, complete disorder. That violent, messy scene is the fray. Over centuries, "fray" stopped being used only for physical battles and started being used for any kind of intense, heated conflict — an argument, a competition, a debate, a political battle, anything that feels like a war.

"Enter" simply means to go into or join something.

Put them together: Enter the fray = to step into a fight or competition that is already happening and become an active participant in it.
The Literal Origin

Centuries ago, this phrase was used in a completely literal sense. In medieval warfare, a battle was called "the fray." Knights and soldiers would be told to enter the fray — meaning, to charge into the battle that was already raging. It was a dramatic, dangerous act. You were leaving a place of safety and throwing yourself into chaos and conflict.

This is why the phrase carries a sense of boldness or decisiveness even today. When you "enter the fray," you are not timidly watching from the sidelines. You are actively choosing to jump in.
How the Meaning Evolved

Over time, as language always does, the word "fray" softened. It no longer had to mean a physical sword fight. Today, "the fray" refers to any situation that is intense, competitive, or contentious, such as:

  • A heated political debate
  • A fierce business competition
  • A public argument or controversy
  • A sports competition
  • An online dispute

And so, "enter the fray" evolved with it. Today you can "enter the fray" in a boardroom, on a sports field, in a courtroom, or even in a comment section on the internet.
The Feeling and Tone of the Idiom

This is important — the idiom carries a specific emotional tone. It suggests:

  • Action and decisiveness — The person is not passive. They are making a deliberate choice to get involved.
  • Awareness of risk or challenge — "The fray" is never a comfortable place. Whoever "enters" it knows things will get difficult.
  • A sense of drama — The phrase has a slightly dramatic, sometimes even heroic, flavour to it. It is not a neutral phrase. It suggests that getting involved is a big deal.

Because of this dramatic quality, the idiom is often used in news articles, speeches, sports commentary, and political writing — places where stakes feel high.
Real-Life Examples (From Different Contexts)

Here are examples that show how the phrase is used across different situations. Read each one and notice how the meaning stays the same even though the situation changes:

Politics:
"After months of silence, the veteran senator finally entered the fray and announced his candidacy for president."
→ He joined the political competition that was already underway.

Business:
"Several small companies had been competing in the smartphone market for years. When Apple entered the fray, everything changed."
→ Apple joined the already-existing, intense competition.

Sports:
"With the team struggling in the second half, the coach substituted his star player, who entered the fray and scored two goals."
→ The star player joined the match (which was already in progress and intense) and made an impact.

A debate or argument:
"The two neighbours had been arguing for hours when the landlord entered the fray."
→ The landlord joined a conflict that was already happening.

Personal life:
"She had been watching the online argument from the sidelines but finally entered the fray and shared her opinion."
→ She stopped watching and became an active participant.
Important Nuances to Remember

1. It implies something was already happening.
You don't "enter the fray" to start something. The fray already exists. You join it. This is a subtle but important point. If you are the one who starts the fight, you would not typically use this phrase.

2. It implies the situation is intense or competitive, not mild.
You wouldn't say "I entered the fray" just because you joined a casual conversation. The situation must feel like a battle — emotionally, competitively, or literally.

3. It does not always have a negative meaning.
Entering the fray is not automatically a bad thing. A hero entering a battle is entering the fray. A great player entering a sports match is entering the fray. It can be admirable or heroic, depending on context. The phrase is neutral in terms of whether the action is good or bad — it just describes what is happening.

4. The phrase focuses on the moment of joining, not the outcome.
"Enter the fray" describes the act of getting involved, not what happens afterward. It captures that specific moment of stepping in.
Common Variations You Will Encounter

The word "fray" does not only appear in this idiom. You will also see it used in related expressions:

  • "In the thick of the fray" — Being right in the middle of the intense action or conflict.
  • "Back into the fray" — Returning to a fight or competition after a break.
  • "Throw yourself into the fray" — Very similar to "enter the fray," but with more emphasis on doing so energetically and without holding back.
  • "Stay out of the fray" — To deliberately choose not to get involved.
  • "Above the fray" — To be so calm, dignified, or powerful that you are not affected by the noise and conflict going on below you. (Often used to describe leaders or people who seem untouched by controversy.)

Of all of these, "enter the fray" and "above the fray" are the two you will encounter most often.
How to Use It Yourself

When you want to say that someone (or you) has decided to join an intense situation, competition, or argument that was already going on, you can use "enter the fray."

Formula: [Person/Group] + entered/enters/will enter + the fray

  • "She entered the fray."
  • "The company is about to enter the fray."
  • "He refused to enter the fray."
  • "When will they enter the fray?"

You can also add when or how:

  • "She entered the fray with a powerful speech."
  • "He entered the fray at the worst possible moment."
What "Enter the Fray" is NOT

To make sure there is no confusion:

  • It does not mean to cause trouble or start conflict from scratch.
  • It does not mean to watch or observe a fight. (That would be the opposite — staying out of the fray.)
  • It does not have to involve physical violence in modern usage. That is only its ancient, literal meaning.
A Quick Memory Trick

Picture a medieval battlefield. Soldiers are already fighting — swords clashing, chaos everywhere. Now imagine a knight on horseback, watching from a hill. He takes a deep breath, lowers his lance, and charges into the battle.

That moment — the charge into the battle — is entering the fray.

Now replace the battlefield with a political debate, a business competition, or an argument. The knight is now a politician, a company, or a person. The moment they decide to stop watching and actively join the intense struggle — that is still entering the fray.
Summary

IdiomEnter the fray
Core meaningTo join an intense fight, competition, or conflict that is already happening
ToneDramatic, bold, decisive
OriginLiteral medieval warfare — charging into battle
Used inPolitics, business, sports, debates, any competitive or contentious situation
Key nuanceThe conflict must already be in progress; you are joining, not starting it

That is everything you need to know about "enter the fray" — from its roots on an ancient battlefield to how it lives in language today. You now understand it better than most native speakers consciously do.
5343: "Enterprise" is a word that carries a sense of ambition and action. Whether it refers to a project, a business, or a personal quality, the word always implies something that takes courage, effort, and a willingness to push forward — often into uncertain or challenging territory. Keep this feeling in mind as you read through the meanings below, because it ties all of them together.

1. A bold or ambitious project, plan, or undertaking

This is the oldest and most fundamental meaning. An "enterprise" in this sense is a task or venture that someone decides to take on — particularly one that is large, difficult, risky, or requires significant effort and planning.

It is not used for small, ordinary tasks. You would not say "cooking breakfast was quite an enterprise" (unless you are being humorous). The word carries weight. It suggests something that matters, something that demands courage or commitment.

Examples:

  • "Sending humans to Mars is a remarkable enterprise."
  • "Building a hospital in a remote region was a challenging enterprise."
  • "The search for a cure was a scientific enterprise that took decades."

Notice that the enterprise could be noble, dangerous, creative, or commercial — the word itself does not judge it. It simply tells you that this is a serious, significant undertaking.

2. A business, company, or commercial organization

In the world of business and economics, "enterprise" is simply another word for a company or business — particularly one of some size or importance.

Examples:

  • "She built her enterprise from nothing into a company with 500 employees."
  • "The government offered loans to support small enterprises."
  • "It is a family enterprise, passed down through three generations."

Here, "enterprise" is essentially a slightly more formal or elevated synonym for "business" or "company." It often appears in official, legal, or economic contexts.

This meaning also extends to business activity in general — not just a single company, but the broader world of commercial work. This is why you'll often see phrases like:

Free enterprise — This refers to an economic system in which private businesses are free to operate, compete, and make profit with little or no government interference. The idea is that the "market" — buyers and sellers — decides what gets made and sold, not the government. The United States is often cited as an example of a free-enterprise economy.

Private enterprise — This refers to businesses owned and operated by private individuals or corporations, as opposed to businesses owned and run by the government (which would be called "public" or "state-owned"). When someone says "the government should leave this to private enterprise," they mean private businesses should handle it, not the state.

Enterprise software / enterprise technology — You may also encounter "enterprise" used as a modifier in the tech industry. "Enterprise software" means software designed for large organizations with complex needs — think of tools used by banks, hospitals, or multinational companies rather than individual users.

3. The quality of initiative, boldness, and resourcefulness in a person

This is a more abstract meaning, but equally important. When "enterprise" refers to a quality that a person has, it means the ability and willingness to come up with ideas, take initiative, work hard, and tackle challenges creatively and boldly — especially in situations where others might hesitate or wait to be told what to do.

A person who shows enterprise does not wait for opportunities to fall into their lap. They go out and create them. They think independently, act decisively, and are not afraid of risk.

Examples:

  • "The young engineer showed remarkable enterprise in designing a solution nobody else had thought of."
  • "What impressed the committee most was her enterprise and determination."
  • "The project succeeded because of the team's enterprise and creativity."

This meaning is why you will sometimes see "enterprise" used in educational and professional contexts to describe a desirable skill — the kind of drive and resourcefulness that makes a person effective and valuable.

These meanings are not random — they all grow from the same root idea: doing something ambitious with courage and initiative.

  • A bold project is an enterprise because it requires courage and effort to pursue.
  • A business is an enterprise because starting and running one requires initiative, risk-taking, and hard work.
  • The personal quality of enterprise is exactly the spirit — the boldness and drive — that makes the first two possible.

So when you see the word "enterprise," ask yourself: is it referring to a thing being done (a project), an organization doing things (a business), or the spirit that drives doing (a quality)? The context will make it clear, and all three will feel natural once you have internalized the core idea of ambitious, courageous action.

"Enterprise" sounds more serious and elevated than its synonyms. If you say "business" or "project," you are being neutral. If you say "enterprise," you are subtly suggesting something grander, more ambitious, or more consequential. Writers and speakers choose "enterprise" when they want to give something a sense of importance or scale.

It can be positive or neutral — rarely negative on its own. Saying something is "a dangerous enterprise" or "a criminal enterprise" does involve negative ideas, but those come from the adjective ("dangerous," "criminal"), not from "enterprise" itself. The word on its own is neutral-to-positive, often carrying admiration.

"A criminal enterprise" — this is a common phrase worth noting specifically. It refers to an organized group of people working together to carry out illegal activities. It treats crime like a business: structured, ongoing, and coordinated. You will see this phrase in legal and journalistic contexts.

Once you have the image of someone bold, driven, and ambitious — launching a project, building a company, or simply refusing to sit still and wait — you have understood "enterprise" completely.
5344:
If someone is enterprising, it means they are the kind of person who spots an opportunity, takes initiative, and boldly finds a way to make something happen — especially when it isn't easy, when others haven't thought of it, or when there's some risk involved.

Think of an enterprising person as someone who doesn't sit around waiting for good things to come to them. They go out and create those good things themselves.
Breaking It Down — What the Word Really Means

Being enterprising is actually a combination of several qualities packed into one word. When you call someone enterprising, you are saying they have all of the following at once:

1. Initiative
They don't need to be told what to do or pushed to act. They see something that could be done and they simply do it on their own.

2. Resourcefulness
They are creative about how they get things done. If one path is blocked, they find another. They use whatever they have available to solve problems.

3. Boldness
They are willing to take risks and try things that haven't been done before, or that others might be too cautious to attempt.

4. Drive and energy
They are not passive. They actively pursue their goals with real effort and enthusiasm.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine two students whose school canteen is selling the same boring sandwiches every day and students are complaining.

  • Student A thinks, "Someone should do something about this." Then goes home and forgets about it.
  • Student B thinks, "I could survey students about what food they want, write a proposal, present it to the school principal, and suggest new options." Then actually does it.

Student B is enterprising.

The enterprising person is the one who turns a problem or an opportunity into action. They don't just recognise the situation — they do something about it, cleverly and boldly.

"Enterprising" is almost always used as a compliment. It praises someone for being proactive, clever, and courageous in pursuing goals.

It is most commonly used to describe:

  • A person — their character or personality
  • A young person — especially someone who shows impressive drive at an early age
  • A specific act or decision — when someone does something particularly creative and bold

Example sentences:

  • "The enterprising teenager set up a small business selling handmade crafts online and made enough money to fund her college fees."
  • "It was an enterprising idea to turn the empty rooftop into a vegetable garden."
  • "He was so enterprising that by the age of 25, he had already launched three successful projects."
  • "The enterprising young chef turned a tiny street stall into a popular restaurant within two years."
What Makes "Enterprising" Different from Similar Words

Several words seem close in meaning but are not quite the same:

  • Hardworking — A hardworking person puts in a lot of effort. But they may simply be following instructions very well. An enterprising person goes beyond that — they spot and create opportunities by themselves.
  • Ambitious — An ambitious person strongly wants to succeed and reach great heights. But wanting something and actually going out to make it happen cleverly are two different things. An enterprising person is ambitious plus they are actively resourceful and bold enough to do something about it.
  • Clever/Smart — Being clever is about thinking well. Being enterprising is about acting well — turning good thinking into real-world results.
  • Brave/Bold — Bravery is about courage. Enterprising includes boldness but it adds creativity and initiative on top of it.

If you want a single phrase that captures all of it: an enterprising person is a resourceful self-starter who boldly turns ideas and opportunities into reality.

When someone is called enterprising, it carries a warm, admiring tone. It suggests you are impressed by the person. It signals that they are someone who makes things happen, someone you would trust to take on a challenge and find a way through.

It is especially powerful when used to describe someone who has done something impressive despite limited resources, experience, or support — because the word implies they found a way regardless.
One Final Way to Lock It In

Think of the noun "enterprise" — which means a bold, ambitious project or business venture. If someone is enterprising, it means they are the kind of person who naturally runs toward enterprises — who naturally takes on big, bold, creative challenges with energy and clever thinking.

They don't wait. They don't make excuses. They find a way.
5345:
To enthrall someone means to capture their attention so completely and powerfully that they feel almost unable to look away, think of anything else, or break free from the experience. The person becomes deeply, almost helplessly fascinated.

Think of it this way: there's a difference between liking a movie and being so absorbed in it that you forget you're sitting in a chair, forget to check your phone, and feel a little stunned when it ends. The second experience? That's being enthralled.

Being enthralled is not mild interest. It is not even strong interest. It is a state of total captivation — as if something has grabbed hold of your mind and is holding it still. The word carries a sense of being under a spell, of having no real desire or ability to pull yourself away.

It describes a surrender of attention that feels almost involuntary.

Historically, "enthrall" also meant to literally enslave someone — to make them a prisoner or servant under another's total power. While this meaning is now rare and mostly found in old books or formal writing, it gives you a sense of where the modern meaning comes from. When something enthralls you today, it "enslaves" your attention, in a metaphorical sense. Your mind becomes its captive.

You can use "enthrall" in two directions:

1. Something enthralls a person:
The subject does the captivating, the person is the one being captivated.

"The ballet performance enthralled the entire audience."
"His storytelling enthralls everyone who listens."

2. A person is enthralled by something:
Here, the person is described as being in that captivated state.

"She was completely enthralled by the documentary."
"The children were enthralled by the magician."

Notice that "enthralled" is very often followed by by or, sometimes, with:

"enthralled by the music" / "enthralled with the idea"
The Different Forms of the Word

FormExample
enthrall (base verb)"Great stories enthrall us."
enthralls (he/she/it)"She enthralls every audience."
enthralled (past tense / past participle)"I was enthralled by the film."
enthralling (ongoing action / describing something)"It was an enthralling performance."
enthrallment (noun)"His enthrallment with chess never faded."

(Note: "Enthralling" is very commonly used as an adjective to describe something that captivates people — a book, a speech, a view, a person.)

Think of fascination on a scale:

interested → engaged → fascinated → captivated → enthralled

"Enthralled" sits at the top. It is more intense than saying someone is "interested" or even "fascinated." It implies a deep, consuming, almost overwhelmed state of attention.

Almost anything that holds deep fascination:

  • A piece of music, a film, a book, a painting, a speech
  • A place, a landscape, a view
  • A person (their charm, talent, or personality)
  • An idea, a subject, a mystery
  • A performance, a story, a conversation

"The night sky enthralled the young astronomer."
"Visitors are enthralled by the ancient ruins."
"The novel enthralled millions of readers worldwide."
"He was so enthralled with the idea that he forgot to eat."
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

• Captivate — very close to enthrall, but slightly lighter. Something that captivates draws you in; something that enthralls holds you completely.
  • Mesmerize — focuses on being almost hypnotized, like staring blankly, locked in. Slightly more about being frozen or dazed.
  • Fascinate — broad and common. Enthrall is a more powerful, elevated version.
  • Spellbind — nearly identical to enthrall; implies being held as if by magic.
  • Rivet — more about sharp, intense focus (often used with attention: "riveted to the spot"). Less emotional warmth than enthrall.

• bore — to cause zero interest
  • repel — to push someone away
  • tire — to drain someone's interest

To enthrall is to hold someone's mind and attention in a state of total, deep, almost spellbound fascination — so completely that they are mentally "captured" by the experience.

If something enthralls you, you are not just enjoying it. You are lost in it.
5346:
The simplest way to put it:
When someone is enthralled, they are so completely and deeply fascinated by something that their entire attention is captured — almost as if they're under a spell. Nothing else exists for them in that moment.

To be enthralled is to be in a state of total, joyful absorption. Your mind is not wandering. You are not half-paying attention. You are 100% locked in — pulled entirely into something that feels wonderful, magical, or extraordinary.

Think of a child watching a magician perform impossible tricks on stage. Their eyes are wide. Their mouth might be slightly open. They don't notice the people sitting next to them, they don't feel hungry, they don't check the time. They are just there, fully and completely, held by what they're witnessing. That child is enthralled.

Being enthralled is an experience of deep pleasure combined with total captivation. There are two elements working together:

  1. You are completely absorbed — your attention is not divided. The thing you're watching, reading, listening to, or experiencing has taken you over entirely.
  2. You are loving every second of it — enthralled is almost always a positive word. You are not trapped or forced; you are willingly lost in something.

When you're enthralled, you might lose track of time. You might not notice the world around you. It's the feeling you get when a book is so good you read three chapters without realising it, or when a piece of music sends chills down your spine and you can't move until it's over.

"Enthralled" sits at the far, powerful end of a spectrum of fascination. Think of it this way:

  • Interested → you're paying attention, but casually.
  • Fascinated → your attention is stronger; you're genuinely engaged.
  • Enthralled → you are deeply, completely, almost helplessly captivated. You cannot look away. You don't want to.

It's not a mild word. You wouldn't say "I was a little bit enthralled." That would be like saying "I was a little bit overwhelmed." The word carries weight. When you use enthralled, you are signalling something powerful.

Almost anything that is compelling, beautiful, extraordinary, or deeply engaging. People are most commonly enthralled by:

  • Performances — a concert, a play, a dance, a magic show
  • Stories — a novel, a film, a gripping conversation, a myth
  • Natural wonders — a sunset, a storm, the ocean
  • People — someone whose personality, beauty, or talent is so captivating you can't stop watching them
  • Ideas — a philosophy, a lecture, a discovery that opens up your mind

The key is that whatever it is, it must have done something special enough to hold your full, willing attention in a state of wonder or delight.
The Positive Flavour of the Word

This is important: enthralled is almost always used in a positive or neutral way. It describes pleasure, wonder, or deep appreciation — not fear, anxiety, or discomfort.

If someone was glued to the news because it was horrifying or stressful, you probably wouldn't say they were "enthralled." You'd say they were "gripped," "alarmed," or "riveted." Enthralled carries a feeling of delight and magic with it. It implies the person wants to be held in that state.

Being enthralled is like being in a temporary trance of fascination. It's not a permanent personality trait — it describes what is happening to you right now, in this moment, because of something specific. Once the music stops, the book ends, or the magician walks off stage, you come back to the ordinary world — often wishing you could stay enthralled a little longer.

These will show you exactly how the word sits in context:

  • "The audience was absolutely enthralled by her performance — no one moved until the last note faded."
  • "As a child, I was enthralled by stories of the night sky and distant galaxies."
  • "He spoke so vividly about his travels that we all sat enthralled for an hour."
  • "She picked up the novel on a whim, but found herself so enthralled that she didn't sleep until she'd finished it."
  • "The tourists stood enthralled at the edge of the waterfall, unable to leave."

Notice how in every case, the person isn't just casually interested. They are held, captured, lost in something.

To make the meaning razor-sharp, here's what it should not be confused with:

  • Not the same as "entertained" — entertainment is pleasant but ordinary. Being enthralled is much deeper and more powerful. You can be entertained by a TV commercial; you would not be enthralled by one.
  • Not the same as "excited" — excitement is energetic and outward-facing. Enthralled is more still, inward, absorbing. An enthralled person might look calm on the outside while being completely captivated on the inside.
  • Not the same as "impressed" — being impressed is a quick judgment ("Wow, that was good!"). Being enthralled is a sustained experience that lasts for the entire duration of the thing you are experiencing.

Before you use the word, ask yourself: "Is this person so deeply and joyfully absorbed in something that the whole world has faded away for them?"

If yes — enthralled is exactly the right word.
5347:
When something is enthralling, it is so powerfully interesting, exciting, or beautiful that it completely takes hold of your attention — and holds it so tightly that you almost can't break free even if you tried.

It's not just "nice" or "interesting." It goes much deeper than that. Something enthralling pulls you in, wraps around your mind, and makes the rest of the world feel like it has faded away.

Think about a time when you were reading a book and you looked up at the clock — and three hours had passed without you noticing. Or you were watching a movie and you forgot to eat. Or someone was telling a story and you were leaning forward, eyes wide, barely breathing.

That feeling — that total, helpless, delicious absorption — is what "enthralling" describes.

The person experiencing the enthralling thing is not just paying attention. They are captured. Almost like being under a spell.

Three things make "enthralling" stand out from simpler words like "interesting" or "good":

1. Intensity
It is a strong word. A math problem can be interesting. A puzzle can be fun. But "enthralling" is reserved for things that hit you with real force — things that have genuine power over your mind and emotions.

2. A sense of being held against your will (pleasantly)
The word carries the idea that you couldn't look away even if you wanted to. You are not actively choosing to pay attention — the thing is making you pay attention. This is what separates "enthralling" from "enjoyable." You enjoy a good meal. An enthralling story grabs you by the collar.

3. It is always pleasurable
Being enthralled feels good. This is important. A car crash might hold your attention, but you wouldn't call it enthralling. An enthralling thing captivates you in a way that you welcome and enjoy. There is pleasure in being held by it.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Enthralling?

Almost anything that engages the mind or emotions deeply:

  • A book or story — "The novel was so enthralling that she read it in a single sitting."
  • A film or TV show — "The documentary was enthralling — I didn't check my phone once."
  • A person — "He was an enthralling speaker; nobody in the room moved a muscle."
  • A performance — "The orchestra's final piece was utterly enthralling."
  • A place or view — "The sight of the northern lights was enthralling."
  • A conversation or idea — "They had an enthralling discussion about the nature of dreams."

Think of a scale of attention-grabbing:

Okay → Interesting → Engaging → Fascinating → Enthralling

"Enthralling" sits near the very top. It is not a word you would use for something mildly good. You use it when something is genuinely, deeply compelling — when it moves you, grips you, and stays with you.
Words That Are Close in Meaning

These words all share the same family of meaning, and understanding them helps you feel what "enthralling" means even more clearly:

  • Captivating — holds your attention beautifully (slightly softer than enthralling)
  • Riveting — holds your attention with great intensity, often used for tense or dramatic things
  • Mesmerizing — holds your attention almost like a trance, very hypnotic
  • Spellbinding — holds you as if by magic
  • Gripping — holds on tight, hard to escape; often used for thrillers or suspenseful things

Enthralling overlaps with all of these but has a slightly warmer, richer feeling — it suggests deep fascination combined with pleasure and wonder.

Do not use "enthralling" for small, ordinary things.

❌ "That sandwich was enthralling."
✅ "That sandwich was delicious."

❌ "The bus ride was enthralling."
✅ "The journey through the mountains was enthralling."

Save "enthralling" for moments of genuine, deep captivation. Because it is a strong word, using it well gives your writing real power. Overusing it makes it lose its force.

Enthralling describes something so powerfully interesting, beautiful, or exciting that it captures your full attention completely, holds it tightly, and makes you lose track of everything else — all while making you feel wonderful about it.
5348: To enthrone someone means to officially place them on a throne, making them a king, queen, bishop, or other high ruler. But it also has a powerful figurative use, which we'll get to.

A throne is the special ceremonial chair that a monarch (a king or queen) sits on as a symbol of their royal power. When someone is enthroned, it means they are formally seated on that throne in an official ceremony, which marks the beginning of their reign or authority.

This is not just someone casually sitting in a chair. It is a solemn, public, official act — a declaration to the world that this person now holds the highest power.

"The archbishop enthroned the young king before the entire court."

Here, the archbishop (a senior church official) is performing the act — physically and ceremonially placing the king on the throne. The king becomes the king through this act.

Who does the enthroning?

Usually a person of religious or constitutional authority — a high priest, an archbishop, a council — performs the act of enthroning someone. It is rarely something a ruler does to themselves. Someone of standing grants the throne by performing the ceremony.

Who gets enthroned?

  • Kings and queens (monarchs)
  • In the Christian church — especially the Church of England and Catholic Church — bishops are also enthroned when they formally take their seat (called a "cathedra") in their cathedral. This is a well-established and specific use of the word.

This is where the word becomes truly rich and widely useful.

To enthrone something or someone figuratively means to elevate them to a position of supreme importance, reverence, or unchallenged authority — even when no actual throne exists.

Think of it this way: a throne represents the highest seat of power. So when you "enthrone" something in a figurative sense, you are treating it as if it sits on that highest seat — above everything else, untouchable, dominant.

"The company enthroned profit above all human values."

This means: the company placed profit in the highest, most sacred position — treating it as the ultimate priority, more important than anything else.

"For centuries, that philosophy was enthroned as the only acceptable truth."

This means: that philosophy was treated with such authority and reverence that no one dared question it — it sat, like a ruler, above all competing ideas.
3. Active vs. Passive — How the Word Is Used

You will see enthrone used in two main ways:

Active — someone performs the act on another:

"They enthroned her as the new queen."

(They did the act; she received it.)

Passive — the focus is on the person who receives the honor (this is the more common form):

"She was enthroned as queen in a grand ceremony."
"Reason was enthroned as the highest human virtue during the Enlightenment."

The passive form "was enthroned" or "is enthroned" is extremely common, so get comfortable recognizing it.
4. The Feeling and Weight of the Word

Enthrone is not a neutral, everyday word. It carries significant weight, ceremony, and grandeur. When a writer uses it, they are signaling that:

  • The elevation being described is formal and significant, not casual.
  • The position being granted is supreme — not just important, but the highest.
  • There is often a sense of permanence or deep establishment — something enthroned is not easily moved.

Because of this weight, writers use it very deliberately. If someone says a dictator "enthroned himself" as ruler, the word carries a critical, even ironic tone — implying the ruler seized a kind of sacred authority they perhaps did not deserve.

The direct opposite of enthrone is dethrone — to remove someone from the throne, stripping them of their power or supreme position.

  • "The rebels dethroned the king after the uprising."
  • "The new smartphone dethroned its predecessor as the best on the market."

Knowing this pair — enthrone / dethrone — helps you understand both words more deeply. You cannot be dethroned unless you were first enthroned.

The act or ceremony of enthroning someone is called an enthronement.

"The enthronement of the new archbishop drew thousands of observers."

This is the noun form you'll encounter in news, historical texts, and religious writing.

Enthrone, as a verb, means to formally and officially place someone — a monarch or bishop — on a throne, thereby granting them the highest position of authority through ceremony. Figuratively, it means to elevate any person, idea, or value to a position of supreme, unchallenged importance — to treat something as sitting above all else. The word always carries a sense of ceremony, grandeur, and supreme authority. Its opposite is dethrone, and the act itself is called an enthronement.
5349:
An enthronement is the formal ceremony or act of placing someone on a throne and officially giving them supreme power or authority.

Think of it this way: a throne is not just a fancy chair — it is a symbol of the highest power in a kingdom or a religious institution. The moment someone is officially seated on that throne, in front of witnesses, through a special ceremony, that event is called an enthronement. It is the moment power is formally handed over and recognised by everyone present.

The word has two simple parts working together:

  • En- → means "to put into" or "to place in"
  • Throne → the special seat that represents supreme power
  • -ment → turns the action into a noun (the event or act of doing something)

So literally: the act of placing someone into the throne.
Where You Will Hear This Word

1. Royal / Monarchical Context

This is the most classic use. When a new king or queen takes power, there is often a grand, public ceremony. That ceremony — where the ruler is formally seated on the throne in front of nobles, officials, and citizens — is an enthronement.

"The enthronement of the new king drew crowds from across the kingdom."

You may also know the word coronation — the placing of a crown on a monarch's head. A coronation and an enthronement often happen as part of the same ceremony, but they refer to slightly different moments within it. The coronation is specifically about the crown; the enthronement is specifically about the throne.

2. Religious Context

This is actually where the word enthronement is used most frequently in modern times. In many Christian traditions — such as the Catholic Church, the Anglican Church, the Orthodox Church — when a new senior leader is appointed (a Pope, Archbishop, Bishop, or Patriarch), they are formally seated on their ceremonial chair or throne during a special service. This is called their enthronement.

"The enthronement of the new Archbishop of Canterbury was held at Canterbury Cathedral."

In this context, the throne is not about political power over a country — it is a symbol of spiritual authority and leadership over a community of believers.

3. Figurative / Metaphorical Use

Sometimes, writers and speakers use enthronement in a broader, non-literal sense — to describe placing any person, idea, value, or thing in a position of the highest importance, reverence, or dominance.

"The 20th century saw the enthronement of science as the ultimate authority on truth."

Here, science was not literally placed on a throne. But the word powerfully conveys the idea that science was elevated to the supreme position of trust and respect in how people understood the world.
What Makes an Enthronement Different from Simply "Taking Power"

This is an important distinction. A person can inherit power the moment a previous ruler dies — but the enthronement is the public, ceremonial, formal recognition of that power. It is the ritual that makes it official in the eyes of the world. It involves:

  • A specific location (a cathedral, a palace, a hall)
  • Witnesses (officials, clergy, citizens, dignitaries)
  • Symbolic actions (being seated, receiving objects of authority, taking oaths)
  • A designated moment that everyone agrees marks the beginning of the new reign or leadership

Without an enthronement, the transfer of power may be legally valid but socially and symbolically incomplete.
The Noun in Action — Example Sentences

• "Hundreds of foreign dignitaries attended the enthronement of the new emperor."
  • "The bishop's enthronement was a deeply moving ceremony for the congregation."
  • "The enthronement of personal freedom as the highest social value changed how laws were written."
  • "Photographs from the enthronement were broadcast to millions around the world."
  • "After decades of struggle, her enthronement as queen felt like a historic moment for the nation."

ConceptDetail

To lock this in your memory, here are the key things to hold onto:

  • Enthronement = the formal act or ceremony of placing someone on a throne (real or symbolic).
  • It applies most often to monarchs and senior religious leaders.
  • It is not just taking power — it is the public, ceremonial recognition of power.
  • Figuratively, it means elevating any person, idea, or value to the highest position of importance.
  • It is always a noun — it names the event or act, not the ongoing state of being on the throne (that would be a "reign" or "tenure").
Enthronement is the formal ceremony that marks the moment someone is officially placed in the highest seat of power or authority — whether in a kingdom, a church, or even in the world of ideas.
